title: The blindfolded man
hook: a man left blindfolded far from home, and why Hindus honor the one who unties it
carry: the guru unties the blindfold; you walk
tomorrow: the dying man and the fire ordeal

segments.voice: Yesterday: Being, unseen yet truly here, like salt in water. Your line was tat tvam asi: you are that. Today ends week three of year two.

Honey and rivers, trees and seeds and salt. And still, maybe, Shvetaketu is thinking what anyone would think. Fine. Being is everywhere, and I am that. So why don't I feel it? Why am I still lost? His father doesn't scold him, and doesn't repeat the salt one more time. He tells him about a man led far from home with a cloth tied over his eyes.
screen: `HONEY, RIVERS, TREES, SEEDS, SALT.` → `SO WHY DON'T I FEEL IT?` → `A MAN WITH A CLOTH OVER HIS EYES.`

segments.voice: Suppose, Uddalaka says, someone leads a man away from his home in Gandhara with his eyes covered, and leaves him in a lonely, empty place. The man turns and shouts, east, north, south: I was brought here blindfolded and left here blindfolded! Then someone unties the cloth and says: Gandhara is that way. Go. And the man, asking from village to village, informed and thinking for himself, gets all the way home. In the same way, Uddalaka says, a person who has a teacher knows. Look at who does what. The stranger doesn't carry the man home. He takes off the blindfold and points. The man still has to walk, and ask, and use his own head. And Gandhara was there the whole time; he just couldn't see which way to turn. Uddalaka adds that for such a person, the only delay is until he's released from the body; then he arrives. And the refrain: you are that, Shvetaketu. Here's the teaching, and it's why Hinduism honors the guru so highly. All week, Being was in the honey, the rivers, the seed, the salt, and in you. What's missing isn't the road; it's sight. A guru unties the blindfold. That's why many Hindus bow to a teacher, touch their feet, and give thanks on Guru Purnima: not because the teacher walks for you, but because they showed you which way home is.
screen: `BLINDFOLDED AND LEFT ALONE.` · `SOMEONE UNTIES IT AND POINTS.` · `HE ASKS, VILLAGE BY VILLAGE.` · `WHY HINDUS HONOR THE GURU.` · then, large: `ONE WITH A TEACHER KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who untied a blindfold for you, a teacher, a grandparent, a friend, an author, and see their face; remember what they said or did. They didn't walk the road for you; they pointed, and you walked. Many Hindus bow to a teacher; if you'd like, bow your head to them in your mind, and let gratitude rise if it's there.
Acharyavan, one who has a teacher. Untied and pointed toward Gandhara, he asks his way village by village; so one who has a teacher knows.
Your line: the guru unties the blindfold; you walk. Week three of year two, done.

howItsDone: Hindu traditions give the guru, the teacher, a place of honor, and many communities observe Guru Purnima each year to give thanks to their teachers.
